facts.claim: "Wraith Pinned to the Mist and Other Games" is track 3 on of Montreal's The Sunlandic Twins, released April 12, 2005, and runs 4:15.
The Sunlandic Twins was produced by Kevin Barnes and recorded almost entirely by him in Athens, Georgia and Oslo, Norway, throughout 2004.
Barnes said he made the album pretty much as a solo record, playing everything himself and building it up one instrument at a time.
The album's songs were written and recorded on Barnes's laptop while the band toured Europe, and he finished it in about 10 weeks with minimal outside vocal and instrumental input.
On Song Exploder, Barnes said he built the track with the drum software from Reason, and he described how he layered dense harmonies.
Song Exploder's host calls it the breakout song from the band's breakout seventh album.

Barnes said the verses contain literary references meant to create a more interesting atmosphere than a typical pop song, because the chorus is simple. The title echoes Longfellow's poem "A Wraith in the Mist".
The album title comes from a dream of Barnes's wife Nina, in which the two of them were the only inhabitants of a planet called Sunlandia.
The song was used, with altered words, in Outback Steakhouse commercials. It also appeared in the film Cloverfield and the TV series Weeds. A music video was made for it.

Kevin Barnes founded of Montreal in Athens, Georgia in 1996. The band is associated with the Elephant Six collective. The Sunlandic Twins was its seventh album and moved toward a more electronic, dance-oriented sound.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Athens, Georgia / Elephant Six indie-pop and neo-psychedelic tradition, at the point where Kevin Barnes shifted toward bedroom-recorded, synth-driven dance-pop.

draft:
"Let's pretend we don't exist / Let's pretend we're in Antarctica." It's a strange thing to offer someone you love: let's go somewhere empty and cold and vanish together. Kevin Barnes sings it like the best idea anyone ever had. On **Wraith Pinned to the Mist and Other Games**, disappearing isn't defeat. It's the honeymoon.

The verses do the dressing up. Barnes has said he packed them with literary references because the chorus was so simple, and you can hear the logic. Satyrs, a bride "stripped bare," Tristan and Izolde, a title that echoes Longfellow's "A Wraith in the Mist." These are roles for two people to try on, games in the title's sense. The best line hides in the costume box: "make sure I see white sails." Even while playing the most doomed lovers he can think of, the narrator wants the version where the ship comes home happy.

That fear sits right beside the joy and never gets settled. The bridge imagines growing younger together forever, then admits it seems "too lovely to be true," and answers with "But I know the best things always do." He flips the old warning into a promise, but the warning is still audible underneath. After that the chorus takes over and repeats again and again, as if saying it enough could make the hiding place real. The album's title comes from a dream Barnes's wife Nina had, in which the two of them were the only people on a planet called Sunlandia. This song is that planet with a backbeat.

The sound is clean and dry, close to the ear. A bright electric guitar picks out a repeating arpeggio, the bass walks underneath, and the drums push a steady, medium-fast beat on kick, snare and closed hi-hat. Barnes built that beat in Reason's drum software, recording most of *The Sunlandic Twins* on his own during 2004 in Athens, Georgia and Oslo, often on a laptop while the band toured Europe, one instrument at a time. His voice is clear and medium-high, smooth on the long notes. The song comes out of the Elephant Six orbit in Athens, but it swaps the old psych clutter for tidy, dance-ready pop. It became the band's breakout.

The world found it. It turned up in *Cloverfield* and *Weeds*, and with its words changed it sold steaks for Outback. That's a funny fate for a song that asks to stop existing.

It gives you the giddy, slightly scared feeling of loving someone so much you'd happily vanish with them, and it keeps singing until you almost believe you could.
